goldenHour.pageSubtitle: When the light is good — and which way it falls. The sun's path today, with the golden and blue hours marked.
goldenHour.notApplicable: Doesn't happen at this location on this date
goldenHour.definitionTitle: What are golden hour and blue hour?
goldenHour.definitionBody: Golden hour is when the sun sits between -4° and +6° of the horizon — warm, low, directional light. Blue hour is the deeper twilight from -6° to -4°, when the sky turns cobalt. (Definition: NOAA / U.S. Naval Observatory.)
goldenHour.timezoneNote: Times use your device's local time when using your own location; for a searched location they're approximated from longitude, not the real timezone — can be off by up to an hour near timezone or daylight-saving boundaries.

rankings.pageSubtitle: Average SQM and light pollution ratio by country/region, based on VIIRS satellite data.
rankings.methodologyBody: Avg SQM is the average of a simplified per-pixel SQM estimate (same formula this site's map and location detail panel use) over each country/region's land area, from the annual VIIRS night-light composite — not the same atmospheric propagation model or exact boundary dataset a professional light-pollution atlas would use, so treat differences of a few hundredths as noise. Ratio is the sky-background brightness multiple versus the darkest country/region in this list (10^((darkest − this)/2.5), the standard astronomical magnitude relationship). "Bortle ≤ 4" is the share of that area at Bortle class 4 or darker.

aboutData.pageTitle: About this map and its data
aboutData.pageSubtitle: How the light pollution map is built, what its numbers mean, and where the data comes from.
aboutData.dataStatusBody: The most recent complete NOAA VIIRS annual composite available via Google Earth Engine at the time this map was built. Updating to a newer year requires a source-code change — this map does not refresh on a schedule.
aboutData.producedStep1Body: NOAA's VIIRS Day/Night Band annual composite provides the raw artificial-light radiance for every point on the map.
aboutData.producedStep2Body: A simplified logarithmic formula converts that radiance into an SQM-like brightness value. This is a deliberately simplified approximation — not the real atmospheric radiative-transfer model that professional light-pollution atlases (e.g. Falchi & Cinzano's World Atlas) use.
aboutData.producedStep3Body: SQM is the more precise comparison value. Bortle class is a simplified, commonly-cited reference derived from that modeled brightness — not a direct field observation.
aboutData.limitsBody: Actual observing conditions also depend on clouds, aerosols, snow, moonlight, temporary lighting, terrain, and local obstructions. A modeled value should not be treated as a live field measurement or a guarantee of visibility. For trip planning, combine this map with its built-in weather, moon-phase, and clear-nights tools and, where possible, an on-site check.
aboutData.otherFeaturesBody: The nighttime weather score, exposure calculator, clear-nights climate stat, and directional sky brightness chart are all clearly-labeled simplified estimates built from free public data (Open-Meteo, NOAA) — not precise forecasts or measurements. Each one explains its own approximation where it's shown.
aboutData.sourceViirs: NOAA VIIRS annual nighttime-light composite — primary light-pollution input.
aboutData.sourceBortle: The Bortle Dark-Sky Scale — public reference for the classification shown on the map.
aboutData.sourceOpenMeteo: Open-Meteo — free weather forecast and historical archive API, powers the nighttime weather and clear-nights features.
aboutData.sourceNoaaSwpc: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center — OVATION aurora model, powers the aurora probability layer.
aboutData.sourceHyg: HYG star database (Hipparcos/Yale/Gliese-Jahreiss, CC BY-SA 4.0) — position and magnitude data for the ~8,900 naked-eye stars on the star map page.
aboutData.sourceD3Celestial: d3-celestial (Olaf Frohn, BSD-3-Clause) — constellation line figures and bilingual names on the star map page.
aboutData.sourceAstronomyEngine: Astronomy Engine (MIT) — the library computing Sun/Moon/planet positions and sidereal time on the star map page.
aboutData.contactBody: This is an independent, non-commercial practice project. Questions, corrections, or feedback are welcome by email.

clearSkyMap.pageSubtitle: Historical share of clear nights by month for any location — plan the best season to visit, not just the best night.
clearSkyMap.chartCaption: Share of nights with mostly clear skies (average night-time cloud cover ≤30%) for each calendar month, based on the last 5 years of Open-Meteo historical archive data — a climate estimate, not a forecast for any specific night.
clearSkyMap.definitionBody: For each calendar month, this averages night-time cloud cover across the last 5 years at this location (same night-bucketing method the live weather forecast uses) and reports the share of nights at or under 30% average cloud cover. It's a screening tool for seasonal patterns, not a promise about any particular night — always check a short-range forecast before you travel.

infoPanel.title: Light Pollution Map FAQ
infoPanel.intro: A light pollution map and dark sky finder — click anywhere to see the Bortle Scale rating and best nearby stargazing spots.

qa.question: What is this light pollution map and how does it work?
qa.answer: This light pollution map (also called a dark sky map or light map) uses satellite-derived night-light data to show artificial skyglow anywhere on Earth. It works as an interactive light pollution map — click any point on the world light pollution map to see a detailed brightness reading for that exact location, from heavily lit cities down to the darkest rural skies.

qa.question: What is the Bortle Scale, and how is sky brightness (SQM) measured?
qa.answer: The Bortle Scale (also called bortle class or bortle rating) is a 9-level scale from Bortle 1 (the darkest possible sky, Milky Way clearly visible) to Bortle 9 (inner-city skies where only the brightest stars show). It's built on top of SQM (Sky Quality Meter) readings — a more precise sky quality measurement in magnitudes per square arcsecond. Click anywhere on the map to instantly check what bortle am i in, without needing a physical darkness scale meter.

qa.question: How do I find dark skies or zero-light-pollution places near me?
qa.answer: Use the map as a dark sky finder or dark site finder to locate the lowest light pollution near me — look for the darkest shading on the map, which marks certified dark sky places, dark sky parks, and other places with no light pollution. True zero light pollution is rare, but Bortle 1–2 areas away from major cities come very close, making them the best spots for genuinely dark, unpolluted skies.

qa.question: What does the sky look like without light pollution, and how is light pollution measured, caused, and reduced?
qa.answer: Under a truly dark night sky without light pollution, thousands of stars, the Milky Way, and faint nebulae become visible — compare your area's light pollution levels on the map against a Bortle 1 site to see the difference. Light pollution is measured with an SQM or estimated from satellite data (this map's method for how to measure light pollution), and skyglow can travel over 100 km from a city, so how far does light pollution travel matters when picking a site. Common examples of light pollution include streetlights, signage, and unshielded fixtures — together they cause light contamination that raises sky brightness citywide. On a practical level, shielded fixtures and warmer lighting are the main way communities reduce light pollution over time.

qa.question: How can I use this map for stargazing, Milky Way viewing, and astrophotography?
qa.answer: Use the map as a stargazing map to plan trips: a milky way visibility map reading of Bortle 4 or darker (ideally during a new moon) tells you how to view the milky way clearly. For astrophotography, brighter skies push you toward shorter sub-exposures — check the map's light pollution reading before taking night sky photos to pick a starting exposure time.

qa.question: Can I check meteor shower or aurora visibility on this map?
qa.answer: Yes — combine the darkness map with a meteor shower forecast to find both a dark viewing spot and the shower's radiant direction. For the northern lights, enable the aurora probability layer to see current visibility odds for your latitude, then cross-reference with the map to avoid local skyglow.

qa.question: Do you have light pollution maps for specific US states or cities?
qa.answer: Yes — search directly for any location in the map's search bar, from broad regions like light pollution map texas or light pollution map california down to specific cities such as light pollution in nyc or las vegas light pollution, and the map will fly straight to that spot with its Bortle and SQM readings. A dedicated regional browse page is planned for the future.

infoPanel.title: Bortle Scale Map FAQ
infoPanel.intro: New to the Bortle scale map? Here's what you need to know.

qa.question: What is the Bortle scale?
qa.answer: The Bortle scale (formally the Bortle dark sky scale) is a 9-level scale created by astronomer John Bortle in 2001 to rate how dark or light-polluted the night sky is at a location, from Class 1 (pristine) to Class 9 (inner-city).

qa.question: What does each Bortle class mean?
qa.answer: Class 1–2 are excellent dark-sky sites where the Milky Way casts shadows; Class 4–6 are suburban skies where only bright stars are visible; Class 7–9 are urban skies where light pollution hides most of the night sky.

qa.question: How do I use this Bortle scale map?
qa.answer: Zoom or search any address on the bortle map — the color overlay shows the estimated Bortle class for that spot based on satellite light pollution data.

qa.question: How does this Bortle scale map actually work?
qa.answer: The map starts from NOAA's VIIRS satellite data, which measures artificial light radiance from space. A simplified logarithmic formula converts that radiance into an SQM-like brightness value, and the Bortle class shown is a simplified reference derived from that modeled value — not a live field measurement or a full atmospheric model like the professional World Atlas.

qa.question: Is this Bortle map accurate?
qa.answer: It's a modeled estimate, not a precise scientific measurement — real sky conditions also depend on clouds, moonlight, and local terrain. SQM is the more precise comparison value, and Bortle class here is best used as a quick, easy-to-read reference for planning, not a guarantee of what you'll see.

qa.question: What's the difference between Bortle scale and SQM?
qa.answer: SQM (Sky Quality Meter) gives a modeled brightness reading in mag/arcsec², while the bortle dark sky scale groups that value into 9 simple categories — this map converts the modeled SQM value into a Bortle class for easy reading.

qa.question: What Bortle class do I need for stargazing or astrophotography?
qa.answer: Class 1–4 is ideal for viewing faint deep-sky objects and the Milky Way; Class 5–6 still works well for planets, the Moon, and bright astrophotography targets.

qa.question: Who uses this map?
qa.answer: Amateur astronomers planning an observing trip, astrophotographers scouting dark-sky locations, and travelers or campers who want to know if they'll see the Milky Way at their destination all use this bortle map before heading out.

qa.question: Where can I find dark sky locations near me?
qa.answer: Use the bortle map to scan outward from your location for the nearest low-Bortle-class (dark sky) areas — parks and rural regions typically offer the biggest improvement.

infoPanel.title: Dark Sky Map FAQ
infoPanel.intro: Here's what this dark sky map shows and how to read it.

qa.question: What does this dark sky map show?
qa.answer: It displays the estimated darkness of the night sky at any location worldwide, based on satellite-measured light pollution — darker colors indicate less artificial light and better sky visibility.

qa.question: What is the dark sky scale?
qa.answer: The dark sky scale — also known as the Bortle scale — is a 9-level classification of night sky darkness, from Class 1 (pristine, no light pollution) to Class 9 (heavily light-polluted urban sky).

qa.question: How is the dark sky scale rating calculated?
qa.answer: Satellite data measuring artificial light radiance is converted into an estimated sky-brightness value, which is then mapped onto the dark sky scale. It's a simplified model, not a precise field measurement — actual conditions vary with clouds, moonlight, and terrain.

qa.question: What do the different colors on the dark sky map mean?
qa.answer: Each color band corresponds to a range on the dark sky scale — from black/green (Class 1–2, darkest skies) through yellow and orange (Class 5–6, suburban) to red/white (Class 8–9, heavily lit urban areas).

qa.question: What dark sky scale rating is considered good for stargazing?
qa.answer: Class 1–4 offers minimal light interference and clear views of faint objects like the Milky Way; Class 5–6 still supports viewing planets, the Moon, and brighter stars.

qa.question: How accurate is this dark sky map?
qa.answer: The ratings are a modeled estimate rather than an on-site measurement — useful for comparing locations and planning ahead, but local factors on any given night can shift actual visibility.

qa.question: Is this dark sky map limited to certain countries?
qa.answer: No — the dark sky map covers locations globally, so you can check the dark sky scale rating for any city, park, or coordinate on Earth.
